strengths: Well-motivated problem identification with clear trade-off analysis between parameter efficiency and expressivity in existing PEFT methods
Strong theoretical contribution with three rigorous theorems: rank characterization (Theorem 1), parameter efficiency proof (Theorem 2), and approximation error bounds (Theorem 3)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three task categories (commonsense reasoning, dialogue, arithmetic), two models, and extensive baselines with statistical significance testing
Consistent empirical results: TeRA matches HiRA (r=32) performance with 51-64× fewer parameters and outperforms comparable-parameter baselines
Thorough ablation studies validating design choices including tensorization schemes, initialization methods, and factor sharing
Practical advantages including zero inference overhead, minimal storage per adapter, and suitability for large-scale deployment scenarios
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (tensorization + VeRA-style parameterization) rather than introducing fundamentally new ideas
Unaddressed training efficiency: paper explicitly acknowledges time-consuming tensor contractions but provides no empirical wall-clock time comparisons with baselines—critical for practical adoption
Under-specified hyperparameter selection: despite Theorem 3, identifying optimal tensorization schemes still requires sampling; paper provides no principled heuristics or guidelines for practitioners

Insufficient justification for frozen random matrix effectiveness: the core premise that frozen random A^(i) matrices + diagonal scaling matches learned parameters lacks deep theoretical or empirical analysis
Theorem 3 bounds lack practical grounding: approximation error involves hard-to-compute tensor spectral norm and g_max term; no empirical validation of bound tightness or predictive value
Limited experimental scope: only two Llama models tested; no evaluation on GPT, Mistral, or larger models (70B+); only English tasks
Incomplete analysis of design choices: why non-shared factors (Table 8) cause catastrophic failure is explained superficially; connection to random matrix theory underdeveloped

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing a key trade-off between high-rank expressivity and parameter efficiency in PEFT methods
Solid theoretical contributions with Theorems 1-3 providing rank bounds, parameter efficiency guarantees (≤J₁+J₂ for full-rank updates), and approximation error analysis
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple diverse benchmarks (8 commonsense reasoning tasks, dialogue generation, arithmetic reasoning) with two model scales
Strong empirical results: matches HiRA performance with 51-64× fewer parameters; consistently outperforms parameter-matched methods (VeRA, LoRETTA)
Thorough ablation studies validating design choices (tensorization strategies, rank analysis, initialization methods)
Practical method with zero inference overhead that can be merged with base weights; easy to implement
Clear presentation with effective visualizations (particularly Figure 1 bubble chart communicating the performance-rank-efficiency trade-off)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily combines established Tucker decomposition with frozen random factors and diagonal training (conceptually similar to VeRA's approach of freezing factors and training scaling vectors)

Insufficient justification for design choices: practical setting of Rᵢ=Iᵢ lacks strong motivation; no principled method for selecting tensorization schemes; different weight matrices require different tuning (Figure 4)

Incomplete understanding of why the method works: missing intuition for why frozen random factors suffice; Theorem 3's approximation bound is complex with unclear tightness; no analysis of learned diagonal patterns

Limited experimental scope: only attention weights (Wq, Wv) tested, not projection or MLP layers; only Llama models tested; limited to 8B scale; no large-scale experiments; missing training time/memory analysis

Theoretical gaps: Theorem 2 only applies when Rᵢ=Iᵢ but practice uses Rᵢ<Iᵢ; Theorem 3's tensor spectral norm bound lacks practical guidance; no analysis of why frozen random initialization preserves task-specific expressivity

Statistical analysis insufficient: only 5 runs with no confidence intervals or significance tests; some improvements appear marginal (e.g., identical 85.31% in Table 2); no variance analysis across seeds

Reproducibility concerns: no code availability mentioned; small validation set (120 examples) for checkpoint selection; missing implementation details (e.g., automatic tensorization selection); appendix proofs not provided
Missing comparisons: MoRA cited but not experimentally compared; limited analysis of when/why TeRA outperforms alternatives; no failure case analysis or limitations discussion

Incomplete practical guidance: no methodology for selecting tensorization schemes on new architectures; no sensitivity analysis for frozen factor initialization; no guidance on when to use TeRA vs alternatives
